---
title: "Introduction"
---

This book explains, chart by chart, the Python scripts in the
[`python/`](https://github.com/BasBBakkerIMF/OpenAI-API-convert-charts/tree/main/python)
folder of the repository. Each script redraws one chart of the IMF Western
Hemisphere *Regional Economic Outlook* (REO) with
[matplotlib](https://matplotlib.org), the standard Python charting library,
from the data that the pipeline extracted from the Excel chart.

It is written for economists who make charts in Excel or R and want to read,
change or write such scripts in Python. You don't need prior matplotlib
experience. The Python you need is explained as it comes up.

![A chart drawn by `python/fig-3-1.py`](images/python/fig-3-1.png)

## How the book is organised

1. **[The shared layout: `chart_style.py`](chart-style.qmd)** explains the
   module that every script imports. It sets the fonts, places the title and
   the sources note, reads the data and saves the picture. Read it first: it
   is the reason the chart scripts are short.
2. **[Recurring techniques](techniques.qmd)** collects the matplotlib
   building blocks that appear in many charts. Examples are a right-hand
   scale, stacked bars, shaded bands, legends and labels below the axis. The
   chart pages link to it rather than explaining the same thing 38 times.
3. **The charts** has one page per chart, in the order of the REO. Each page
   shows the published chart next to the Python version. It describes the
   data and walks through the script.

The first chart page, [Figure 1.1](charts/fig-1-1.qmd), explains every line.
Later pages concentrate on what is new in that chart.

## Running the scripts

The scripts need the project's virtual environment (see `install.ps1` in the
repository), which has pandas, numpy, openpyxl and matplotlib. In PowerShell,
from the `python` folder:

```powershell
cd python
..\.venv\Scripts\python.exe fig-3-1.py     # one chart
..\.venv\Scripts\python.exe run_all.py     # all 38 charts
```

Each script reads `excel_and_png/<stem>.xlsx` and writes
`python/figures/<stem>.png`. The **stem** is the chart's name, such as
`fig-3-1`, and is used for every file that belongs to that chart. The paths
are relative to the repository, so the scripts work wherever you put it.

::: {.callout-note}
## The scripts are the reference

Every page ends with the complete script under **The complete script**.
`add_full_scripts.py` in this folder copies it in from `python/`. After
changing a script, run it again (`..\.venv\Scripts\python.exe
add_full_scripts.py`) and re-render the book. The shorter excerpts in the
walk-throughs are copied by hand, so if they ever differ from the script, the
script is what runs.
:::

## What a chart script looks like

Every script has the same six parts, in the same order. Here they are for
[Figure 3.1](charts/fig-3-1.qmd), a plain line chart, shortened:

```python
from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart   # 1. imports

STEM = "fig-3-1"
data = read_chart_data(STEM)                                     # 2. the data

series_colours = {"USA": "#0067A5", "CAN": "#454545", ...}       # 3. the series

fig, ax = new_chart(title="Terms of Trade",                      # 4. the frame
                    subtitle="(Index: 2019 = 100)",
                    caption="Sources: ...")

for series, colour in series_colours.items():                    # 5. the drawing
    ax.plot(data["category"], data[series], color=colour, label=series)
ax.set_ylim(90, 125)
ax.legend(loc="upper left")

save_chart(fig, STEM)                                            # 6. save
```

1. **Imports.** Load the helpers from `chart_style.py`, and sometimes a few
   matplotlib tools.
2. **The data.** Read the chart's workbook into a pandas *DataFrame*, a table
   with named columns. `data["USA"]` is the column for the United States.
3. **The series and their colours.** A *dictionary* (`{key: value, ...}`)
   maps each column to its colour. The order of the dictionary is also the
   drawing order and the legend order.
4. **The frame.** `new_chart()` creates the 5 × 5 inch figure with title,
   subtitle and sources. It returns the figure (`fig`) and the plot area
   (`ax`, for *axes*), on which everything else is drawn.
5. **The drawing.** Lines, bars and areas, then the axes (limits, ticks,
   labels) and the legend. This is the only part that differs much between
   charts.
6. **Save** the picture as `python/figures/<stem>.png`.

label tables.

## Why Python versions?

The pipeline produces R scripts, generated by a language model. The Python
scripts were written by converting those R scripts and comparing every
result with the published chart. They are an alternative for colleagues who
work in Python, and a second check of the extracted data. Two charts have
known gaps:

- **Figure 12.1** has no error bars, because the confidence intervals are not
  in the extracted data.
- **Some category labels** are typed into the scripts (for example the region
  names in Figure 9.1), because they are not in the extracted data either.
